analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare-participating hospitals and clinics from forcing nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts or 12-hour caps.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in August 2026 and referred to the Finance Committee; with only four Senate supporters and no hearing or vote, it has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes a nurse-overtime limit a condition of Medicare participation. Hospitals, home health agencies, surgical centers, and clinics could no longer require nurses to work past a scheduled shift, beyond 48 hours a week, past 12 consecutive hours, or during the 10 hours right after a 12-hour shift. Nurses could still volunteer for extra hours, and the limits pause during declared emergencies. The bill also adds whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections, notice and schedule-posting requirements, and fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses at Medicare-participating facilities gain enforceable limits on forced overtime, protection from being fired or reported to licensing boards for refusing it, and the right to complain to Health and Human Services with guaranteed investigations. Patients gain too, because the bill's own findings cite research linking fatigued nurses to medical errors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nurses and the patients they care for

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits providers from requiring nurses to work beyond a previously scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, more than 12 consecutive hours in 24, or during the 10 hours following the 12th hour worked, counting on-call and standby time as hours worked.

Protects nurses who refuse mandatory overtime or report violations from discharge, discipline, pay cuts, or retaliatory reports to state licensing agencies, and requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to investigate nurse complaints.
Lets the Secretary impose civil money penalties up to $10,000 per knowing violation, steeper for repeat violators, and publish the names of penalized providers online.

The bill's findings cite research that nurses working long hours experience fatigue and impaired vigilance that contributes to medical errors, and that 18 states have already restricted mandatory overtime for nurses.
The limits apply only during declared emergencies under defined conditions, and do not preempt state laws that provide stronger protections or affect rights under union contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare providers bear the cost: they can no longer cover vacancies by mandating overtime, so they would need to hire more staff, pay overtime rates to volunteers, or accept unfilled shifts. Some of that cost could reach patients and insurers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Providers lose the ability to fill last-minute vacancies with mandatory overtime, which could raise their labor costs and, in facilities operating on thin margins, show up as higher prices or reduced service hours.

The bill lets nurses keep volunteering for unlimited overtime, so fatigued nurses could still work 16-hour days by choice; enforcement also depends mainly on nurses filing complaints with the Secretary rather than proactive inspections.

The overtime limits are suspended during declared emergencies or disasters if the provider tries to fill the need by other means, which could be a wide window in practice, and the definition excludes emergencies arising from consistent understaffing.
The bill also orders a two-year federal study of safe working-hour standards after the limits take effect, meaning the fixed caps it sets now could later be revised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For nurses and patients, the benefits are direct and concrete: a hard cap on forced overtime, a guaranteed rest window, and real retaliation protections, all enforceable through federal complaints and fines. The main costs fall on providers, who would have to staff shifts with hired workers rather than captive overtime. The bill is a reasonable design rather than a perfect one: voluntary overtime stays legal, the emergency exception is broad, and enforcement leans on complaint-driven investigations. But its immediate practical value is limited by the fact that it has not advanced at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill with Sens. Schiff, Fetterman, and Van Hollen on August 6, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the bill's history after the referral; the Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically alive but has not moved.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, hospitals and other providers have kept the status quo, in which nurses can still be required to work beyond scheduled shifts; nurses and patients have gained nothing because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, so far, keep current staffing practices

sides.party_line_note: The bill has never drawn a vote, and all four of its sponsors are Democrats (4 of 45 Senate Democrats), so no record yet shows how the other 98 senators or any provider groups stand.

industries.note: Hospitals routinely cover vacancies by mandating overtime rather than hiring and scheduling enough staff; the bill removes that option as a condition of Medicare participation and fines knowing violations. Their cost-saving through forced overtime comes at the expense of nurse working conditions and patient safety, so their interest runs against the public's here.

Home health agencies are covered providers under the bill and would face the same overtime caps and documentation requirements, a cost concentrated in an industry that depends on extended visits and on-call time.

industries.industry: Ambulatory surgical centers, rural health clinics, and community health centers
industries.note: These smaller providers are covered too, but the overtime limits mirror rules already adopted in 18 states, and the caps protect their own nursing staffs; the adjustment cost is likely smaller than for hospitals.

analysis.trajectory: This bill was introduced with about two months left in a two-year Congress and has four sponsors, all Democrats, in a chamber Republicans hold 55-45. A bill sitting in the Finance Committee this late with no hearing or markup almost never reaches the floor; the most likely outcome is that it dies when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, and must be reintroduced fresh in the next one.
